analysis.one_liner: Bans unions from requiring workers to pay dues or fees as a condition of employment nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted 98 cosponsors, all Republicans, but never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal labor law so that no employer and union could sign a contract requiring employees to join the union or pay union dues or fees as a condition of keeping their job. It applies nationwide, overriding the laws of states that currently allow such agreements. Supporters call this 'right to work' and say it protects workers who do not want to pay dues. Unions and many labor economists counter that it lets workers benefit from union-negotiated contracts without paying for them, which starves unions of money and is associated with lower wages for union and non-union workers alike.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers gain the most: a weaker union movement means less organized pressure over wages, benefits, and working conditions, and lower labor costs in unionized workplaces. Workers who object to paying union dues would no longer have to pay them, even in workplaces covered by union contracts.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the sections of federal law that let employers and unions sign contracts requiring workers to join the union or pay dues as a condition of employment, and ends the special payroll-deduction authority for railroad carriers [S2].
Its stated purpose is to protect the 'free choice of individual employees' to join or refrain from joining a labor organization [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Labor unions bear the cost: they would have to represent workers under collective bargaining agreements without being able to collect dues or fees from those who decline to pay. Workers who rely on union bargaining power, whether members or not, would likely face weaker negotiating leverage over time.

drawbacks.text: Under federal law, unions must bargain for everyone in a covered workplace, not just paying members; the bill removes the ability to charge non-members for that representation, which is why opponents call it a way to defund unions rather than expand freedom (mechanism explained from the bill text and general labor-law principles) [S3].

The strongest good-faith objection on the other side is that no worker should be forced to financially support an organization as a condition of employment; the bill's own title frames it as protecting free choice [S3].
The bill would have overridden the choices of the many states that currently permit union security agreements, replacing state policy with a single national rule [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For an individual worker who resents paying dues, the bill offers a real, immediate benefit. For workers as a group, the trade is much less favorable: unions would still be legally required to represent everyone but could collect from no one who opts out, shrinking their resources for bargaining, enforcement, and organizing. Research on existing state right-to-work laws generally finds lower wages and union membership in those states. Weighing this honestly, the bill's main structural effect is to shift bargaining power away from organized labor and toward employers, with the dues freedom as the headline benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no hearing or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King of Iowa introduced the bill on May 26, 2011, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S1].
On September 8, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, where it remained [S5].
No further action was taken for the rest of the 112th Congress; the bill never reached the House floor and never received a vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Labor unions and the workers who depend on them are better off, because union security agreements remain legal everywhere and union dues collections were never disrupted. Employers who favored a national right-to-work law did not get one.

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered cosponsors.

for.name: 98 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat cosponsored it.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no hearing, no vote — and referred it to a subcommittee where it sat until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 98 cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican; no Democrats are listed among the cosponsors [S4].

industries.note: The bill would bar union security agreements nationwide, cutting off dues and fees from workers who decline to pay while unions remain obligated to represent them. Unions' interest in staying solvent runs alongside the wage and bargaining interests of the workers they represent.

With weaker union finances and membership, employers would face less organized pressure over wages, benefits, and conditions, and lower labor costs. That gain comes directly out of workers' collective leverage.

The bill would repeal the Railway Labor Act provision letting rail carriers require payroll deduction of union dues under union security agreements, changing long-standing railroad labor arrangements [S2].
